entries.afc3371aeb9feb0e0f707fe87d787ab6dfc30f32: <div sID="gen12484" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="110" osisID="Ps.110" sID="Ps.110"/> <div eID="gen12484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12485" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12486" type="x-p"/> This psalm is pure gospel; it is only, and wholly, concerning Christ, the Messiah promised to the fathers and expected by them. It is plain that the Jews of old, even the worst of them, so understood it, however the modern Jews have endeavoured to pervert it and to rob us of it; for when the Lord Jesus proposed a question to the Pharisees upon the first words of this psalm, where he takes it for granted that David, in spirit, calls Christ his Lord though he was his Son, they chose rather to say nothing, and to own themselves gravelled, than to make it a question whether David does indeed speak of the Messiah or no; for they freely yield so plain a truth, though they foresee it will turn to their own disgrace, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.41-Matt.22.46">Matt. xxii. 41</reference>, &c. Of him therefore, no doubt, the prophet here speaks of him and of no other man. Christ, as our Redeemer, executes the office of a prophet, of a priest, and of a king, with reference both to his humiliation and his exaltation; and of each of these we have here an account. I. His prophetical office, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.2">ver. 2</reference>. II. His priestly office, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">ver. 4</reference>. III. His kingly office, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.5">5,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.6">6</reference>. IV. His estates of humiliation and exaltation, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.7">ver. 7</reference>. In singing this psalm we must act faith upon Christ, submit ourselves entirely to him, to his grace and government, and triumph in him as our prophet, priest, and king, by whom we hope to be ruled, and taught, and saved, for ever, and as the prophet, priest, and king, of the whole church, who shall reign till he has put down all opposing rule, principality, and power, and delivered up the kingdom to God the Father.
entries.cab16db506fbc4f6e7df53ecb9387ea54c6bb37f: <div eID="gen12486" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12485" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Messiah's Dominion.</title> <div sID="gen12487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool. <hi type="super">2</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thy people <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> willing in the day of thy power, in the beauties of holiness from the womb of the morning: thou hast the dew of thy youth. <hi type="super">4</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. <div eID="gen12487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12488" type="x-p"/> Some have called this psalm <hi type="italic">David's creed,</hi> almost all the articles of the Christian faith being found in it; the title calls it <hi type="italic">David's psalm,</hi> for in the believing foresight of the Messiah he both praised God and solaced himself, much more may we, in singing it, to whom that is fulfilled, and therefore more clearly revealed, which is here foretold. Glorious things are here spoken of Christ, and such as oblige us to consider how great he is. <div eID="gen12488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12489" type="x-p"/> I. That he is David's Lord. We must take special notice of this because he himself does. <reference osisRef="Matt.22.43">Matt. xxii. 43</reference>, <hi type="italic">David, in spirit, calls him Lord.</hi> And as the apostle proves the dignity of Melchizedek, and in him of Christ, by this, that so great a man as Abraham was paid him <hi type="italic">tithes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.4">Heb. vii. 4</reference>), so we may by this prove the dignity of the Lord Jesus that David, that great man, <hi type="italic">called him</hi> his <hi type="italic">Lord;</hi> by him that king acknowledges himself to reign, and to him to be acceptable as a servant to his lord. Some think he calls him his <hi type="italic">Lord</hi> because he was the Lord that was to descend from him, his son and yet his Lord. Thus him immediate mother calls him her <hi type="italic">Saviour</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.47">Luke i. 47</reference>); even his parents were his subjects, his saved ones. <div eID="gen12489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12490" type="x-p"/> II. That he is constituted a sovereign Lord by the counsel and decree of God himself: <hi type="italic">The Lord,</hi> Jehovah, <hi type="italic">said unto him, Sit</hi> as a king. He <hi type="italic">receives of the Father</hi> this honour and glory (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.17">2 Pet. i. 17</reference>), from him who is the fountain of honour and power, and <hi type="italic">takes it not to himself.</hi> He is therefore rightful Lord, and his title is incontestable; for what God has said cannot be gainsaid. He is therefore everlasting Lord; for what God has said shall not be unsaid. He will certainly take and keep possession of that kingdom which the Father has committed to him, and none can hinder. <div eID="gen12490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12491" type="x-p"/> III. That he was to be advanced to the highest honour, and entrusted with an absolute sovereign power both in heaven and in earth: <hi type="italic">Sit thou at my right hand.</hi> Sitting is a resting posture; after his services and sufferings, he entered into rest from all his labours. It is a ruling posture; he sits to give law, to give judgment. It is a remaining posture; he sits like a king for ever. Sitting at the right hand of God denotes both his dignity and his dominion, the honour put upon him and the trusts reposed in him by the Father. All the favours that come from God to man, and all the service that comes from man to God, pass through his hand. <div eID="gen12491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12492" type="x-p"/> IV. That all his enemies were in due time to be made his footstool, and not till then; but then also he must reign in the glory of the Mediator, though the work of the Mediator will be, in a manner, at an end. Note, 1. Even Christ himself has enemies that fight against his kingdom and subjects, his honour and interest, in the world. There are those that will not have him to reign over them, and thereby they join themselves to Satan, who will not have him to reign at all. 2. These enemies will <hi type="italic">be made his footstool;</hi> he will subdue them and triumph over them; he will do it easily, as easily as we put a footstool in its proper place, and such a propriety there will be in it. He will make himself easy by the doing of it, as a man that sits with a footstool under his feet; he will subdue them in such a way as shall be most for his honour and their perpetual disgrace; he will <hi type="italic">tread down the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.4.3">Mal. iv. 3</reference>. 3. God the Father has undertaken to do it: <hi type="italic">I will make them thy footstool,</hi> who can do it. 4. It will not be done immediately. All his enemies are now in a chain, but not yet made his footstool. This the apostle observes. <reference osisRef="Heb.2.8">Heb. ii. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">We see not yet all things put under him.</hi> Christ himself must wait for the completing of his victories and triumphs. 5. He shall wait till it is done; and all their might and malice shall not give the least disturbance to his government. His sitting at God's right hand is a pledge to him of his setting his feet, at last, on the necks of all his enemies. <div eID="gen12492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12493" type="x-p"/> V. That he should have a kingdom set up in the world, beginning at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord shall send the rod</hi> or <hi type="italic">sceptre of thy strength out of Zion,</hi> by which thy kingdom shall be erected, maintained, and administered." The Messiah, when he sits on the right hand of the Majesty in the heavens, will have a church on earth, and will have an eye to it; for he is <hi type="italic">King upon the holy hill of Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>), in opposition to Mount Sinai, that frightful mountain, on which the law was given, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18 Heb.12.24 Gal.4.24-Gal.4.25">Heb. xii. 18, 24; Gal. iv. 24, 25</reference>. The kingdom of Christ took rise from Zion, the city of David, for he was the Son of David, and was to have <hi type="italic">the throne of his father David.</hi> By the rod of his strength, or his strong rod, is meant his everlasting gospel, and the power of the Holy Ghost going along with it—the report of the word, and the arm of the Lord accompanying it (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Isa. liii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.16">Rom. i. 16</reference>),—the gospel coming in word, and in power, and <hi type="italic">in the holy Ghost,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">1 Thess. i. 5</reference>. By the word and Spirit of God souls were to be reduced first, and brought into obedience to God, and then ruled and governed according to the will of God. This strong rod God sent forth; he poured out the Spirit, and gave both commissions and qualifications to those that preached the word, and <hi type="italic">ministered the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.5">Gal. iii. 5</reference>. It was sent out of Zion, for there the Spirit was given, and there the preaching of the gospel among all nations must begin, at Jerusalem. See <reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Luke xxiv. 47</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.49">49</reference>. <hi type="italic">Out of Zion</hi> must <hi type="italic">go forth the law</hi> of faith, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 3</reference>. Note, The gospel of Christ, being sent of God, is <hi type="italic">mighty through God</hi> to do wonders, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.4">2 Cor. x. 4</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">the rod of Christ's strength.</hi> Some make it to allude not only to the sceptre of a prince, denoting the glory of Christ shining in the gospel, but to a shepherd's crook, his rod and staff, denoting the tender care of Christ takes of his church; for he is both <hi type="italic">the great and the good Shepherd.</hi> <div eID="gen12493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12494" type="x-p"/> VI. That his kingdom, being set up, should be maintained and kept up in the world, in spite of all the oppositions of the power of darkness. 1. Christ shall rule, shall give laws, and govern his subjects by them, shall perfect them, and make them easy and happy, shall do his own will, fulfil his own counsels, and maintain his own interests among men. His kingdom is of God, and it shall stand; his crown sits firmly on his head, and there it shall flourish. 2. He shall rule <hi type="italic">in the midst of his enemies.</hi> He sits in heaven in the midst of his friends; his throne of glory there is surrounded with none but faithful worshippers of him, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.11">Rev. v. 11</reference>. But he rules on earth in the midst of his enemies, and his throne of government here is surrounded with those that hate him and fight against him. Christ's church is a lily among thorns, and his disciples are sent forth <hi type="italic">as sheep in the midst of wolves;</hi> he knows <hi type="italic">where they dwell, even where Satan's seat is</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.13">Rev. ii. 13</reference>), and this redounds to his honour that he not only keeps his ground, but gains his point, notwithstanding all the malignant policies and powers of hell and earth, which cannot shake the rock on which the church is built. <hi type="italic">Great is the truth, and will prevail.</hi> <div eID="gen12494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12495" type="x-p"/> VII. That he should have a great number of subjects, who should be to him for a name and a praise, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">v. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen12495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12496" type="x-p"/> 1. That they should be his own people, and such as he should have an incontestable title to. They are given to him by the Father, who gave them their lives and beings, and to whom their lives and beings were forfeited. <hi type="italic">Thine they were and thou gavest them me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.6">John xvii. 6</reference>. They are redeemed by him; he has purchased them to be to himself <hi type="italic">a peculiar people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit. ii. 14</reference>. They are his by right, antecedent to their consent. He <hi type="italic">had much people in Corinth</hi> before they were converted, <reference osisRef="Acts.18.10">Acts xviii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen12496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12497" type="x-p"/> 2. That they should be <hi type="italic">a willing people,</hi> a people of willingness, alluding to servants that choose their service and are not coerced to it (they love their masters and would not go out free), to soldiers that are volunteers and not pressed men ("Here am I, send me"), to sacrifices that are free-will offerings and not offered of necessity; we <hi type="italic">present ourselves living sacrifices.</hi> Note, Christ's people are a willing people. The conversion of a soul consists in its being willing to be Christ's, coming under his yoke and into his interests, with an entire compliancy and satisfaction. <div eID="gen12497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12498" type="x-p"/> 3. That they should be so <hi type="italic">in the day of his power, in the day of thy muster</hi> (so some); when thou art enlisting soldiers thou shalt find a multitude of volunteers forward to be enlisted; let but the standard be set up and the <hi type="italic">Gentiles</hi> will <hi type="italic">seek to it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">Isa. xi. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.3">lx. 3</reference>. Or when thou art drawing them out to battle they shall be willing to <hi type="italic">follow the Lamb whithersoever he goes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Rev. xiv. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">In the day of thy armies</hi> (so some); "when the first preachers of the gospel shall be sent forth, as Christ's armies, to reduce apostate men, and to ruin the kingdom of apostate angels, then all that are <hi type="italic">thy people shall be willing;</hi> that will be thy time of setting up thy kingdom." <hi type="italic">In the day of thy strength,</hi> so we take it. There is a general power which goes along with the gospel to all, proper to make them willing to be Christ's people, arising from the supreme authority of its great author and the intrinsic excellency of the things themselves contained in it, besides the undeniable miracles that were wrought for the confirmation of it. And there is also a particular power, the power of the Spirit, going along with the power of the word, to the people of Christ, which is effectual to make them willing. The former leaves sinners without matter of excuse; this leaves saints without matter of boasting. Whoever are willing to be Christ's people, it is the free and mighty grace of God that makes them so. <div eID="gen12498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12499" type="x-p"/> 4. That they should be so <hi type="italic">in the beauty of holiness,</hi> that is, (1.) They shall be allured to him by the beauty of holiness; they shall be charmed into a subjection to Christ by the sight given them of his beauty, who is the holy Jesus, and the beauty of the church, which is the holy nation. (2.) They shall be admitted by him into the beauty of holiness, as spiritual priests, to minister in his sanctuary; for <hi type="italic">by the blood of Jesus we have boldness to enter into the holiest.</hi> (3.) They shall attend upon him in the beautiful attire or ornaments of grace and sanctification. Note, Holiness is the livery of Christ's family and that which <hi type="italic">becomes his house for ever.</hi> Christ's soldiers are all thus clothed; these are the colours they wear. The armies of heaven <hi type="italic">follow him in fine linen, clean and white,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.14">Rev. xix. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen12499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12500" type="x-p"/> 5. That he should have great numbers of people devoted to him. The multitude of the people is the honour of the prince, and that shall be the honour of this prince. <hi type="italic">From the womb of the morning thou hast the dew of thy youth,</hi> that is, abundance of young converts, like the drops of dew in a summer's morning. In the early days of the gospel, in the morning of the New Testament, the youth of the church, great numbers flocked to Christ, and there were <hi type="italic">multitudes that believed,</hi> a <hi type="italic">remnant of Jacob,</hi> that was as <hi type="italic">dew from the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mic. v. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.4 Isa.64.8">Isa. lxiv. 4, 8</reference>. Or thus? "<hi type="italic">From the womb of the morning</hi> (from their very childhood) <hi type="italic">thou hast the dew of thy</hi> people's <hi type="italic">youth,</hi> that is, their hearts and affections when they are young; it is thy youth, because it is dedicated to thee." <hi type="italic">The dew of the youth</hi> is a numerous, illustrious, hopeful show of young people flocking to Christ, which would be to the world as dew to the ground, to make it fruitful. Note, The dew of our youth, even in the morning of our days, ought to be consecrated to our Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen12500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12501" type="x-p"/> 6. That he should be not only a king, but a priest, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">v. 4</reference>. The same Lord that said, <hi type="italic">Sit thou at my right hand, swore, and will not repent, Thou art a priest,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">Be thou a priest;</hi> for by the word of his oath he was consecrated. Note, (1.) Our Lord Jesus Christ is a priest. He was appointed to that office and faithfully executes it; he is <hi type="italic">ordained for men in things pertaining to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sin</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.1">Heb. v. 1</reference>), to make atonement for our sins and to recommend our services to God's acceptance. He is God's minister to us, and our advocate with God, and so is a Mediator between us and God. (2.) He is <hi type="italic">a priest for ever.</hi> He was designed for a priest, in God's eternal counsels; he was a priest to the Old-Testament saints, and will be a priest for all believers to the end of time, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.8">Heb. xiii. 8</reference>. He is said to be <hi type="italic">a priest for ever,</hi> not only because we are never to expect any other dispensation of grace than this by the priesthood of Christ, but because the blessed fruits and consequences of it will remain to eternity. (3.) He is made a priest with an oath, which the apostle urges to prove the pre-eminence of his priesthood above that of Aaron, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.20-Heb.7.21">Heb. vii. 20, 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord has sworn,</hi> to show that in the commission there was no implied reserve of a power of revocation; for <hi type="italic">he will not repent,</hi> as he did concerning Eli's priesthood, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.30">1 Sam. ii. 30</reference>. This was intended for the honour of Christ and the comfort of Christians. The priesthood of Christ is confirmed by the highest ratifications possible, that it might be an unshaken foundation for our faith and hope to build upon. (4.) He is a priest, not of the order of Aaron, but of that of Melchizedek, which, as it was prior, so it was upon many accounts superior, to that of Aaron, and a more lively representation of Christ's priesthood. Melchizedek was <hi type="italic">a priest upon his throne,</hi> so is Christ (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zech. vi. 13</reference>), king of righteousness and king of peace. Melchizedek had no successor, nor has Christ; his is an unchangeable priesthood. The apostle comments largely upon these words (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.1-Heb.7.28">Heb. vii.</reference>) and builds on them his discourse of Christ's priestly office, which he shows was no new notion, but built upon this most sure word of prophecy. For, as the New Testament explains the Old, so the Old Testament confirms the New, and Jesus Christ is the Alpha and Omega of both.
entries.5ad47e428b298184bdb7877c22d75cb90c50b177: <div eID="gen12501" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Messiah's Dominion.</title> <div sID="gen12502" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> The Lord at thy right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath. <hi type="super">6</hi> He shall judge among the heathen, he shall fill <hi type="italic">the places</hi> with the dead bodies; he shall wound the heads over many countries. <hi type="super">7</hi> He shall drink of the brook in the way: therefore shall he lift up the head. <div eID="gen12502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12503" type="x-p"/> Here we have our great Redeemer, <div eID="gen12503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12504" type="x-p"/> I. Conquering his enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.5-Ps.110.6">v. 5, 6</reference>) in order to the making of them <hi type="italic">his footstool,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">v. 1</reference>. Our Lord Jesus will certainly bring to nought all the opposition made to his kingdom, and bring to ruin all those who make that opposition and persist in it. He will be too hard for those, whoever they may be, that fight against him, against his subjects and the interest of his kingdom among men, either by persecutions or by perverse disputings. Observe here, <div eID="gen12504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12505" type="x-p"/> 1. The conqueror: <hi type="italic">The Lord—Adonai,</hi> the Lord Jesus, he to whom all judgment is committed, he shall make his own part good against his enemies. <hi type="italic">The Lord at thy right hand, O church!</hi> so some; that is, the Lord that is nigh unto his people, and a very present help to them, that is at their right hand, to strengthen and succour them, shall appear for them against his and their enemies. See <reference osisRef="Ps.109.31">Ps. cix. 31</reference>. <hi type="italic">He shall stand at the right hand of the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.16.8">Ps. xvi. 8</reference>. Some observe that when Christ is said to do his work at the right hand of his church it intimates that, if we would have Christ to appear for us, we must <hi type="italic">bestir ourselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.24">2 Sam. v. 24</reference>. Or, rather, <hi type="italic">At thy right hand, O God!</hi> referring to <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">v. 1</reference>, in the dignity and dominion to which he is advanced. Note, Christ's sitting at the right hand of God speaks as much terror to his enemies as happiness to his people. <div eID="gen12505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12506" type="x-p"/> 2. The time fixed for this victory: <hi type="italic">In the day of his wrath,</hi> that is, the time appointed for it, when the measure of their iniquities is full and they are ripe for ruin. When the day of his patience has expired, when the day of his wrath comes. Note, (1.) Christ has wrath of his own, as well as grace. It concerns us to <hi type="italic">kiss the Son,</hi> for he can be <hi type="italic">angry</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">Ps. ii. 12</reference>) and we read of the <hi type="italic">wrath of the Lamb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Rev. vi. 16</reference>. (2.) There is a day of wrath set, a year of <hi type="italic">recompences for the controversy of Zion, the year of the redeemed.</hi> The time is set for the destruction of particular enemies, and when that time shall come it shall be done, how unlikely soever it may seem; but the great day of his wrath will be at the end of time, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.17">Rev. vi. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen12506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12507" type="x-p"/> 3. The extent of this victory. (1.) It shall reach very high: He <hi type="italic">shall strike through kings.</hi> The greatest of men, that set themselves against Christ, shall be made to fall before him. Though they be <hi type="italic">kings of the earth,</hi> and rulers, accustomed to carry their point, they cannot carry it against Christ, they do but make themselves ridiculous by the attempt, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.2-Ps.2.5">Ps. ii. 2-5</reference>. Be their power among men ever so despotic, Christ will call them to an account; be their strength ever so great, their policies ever so deep, Christ will be too hard for them, and wherein they deal proudly he will be above them. Satan is the prince of this world, Death the king of terrors, and we read of kings that make war with the Lamb; but they shall all be brought down and broken. (2.) It shall reach very far. The trophies of Christ's victories will be set up <hi type="italic">among the heathen,</hi> and in many countries, wherever any of his enemies are, not his eye only, but his <hi type="italic">hand, shall find them out</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.8">Ps. xxi. 8</reference>) and his wrath shall follow them. He will <hi type="italic">plead with all nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Joel.3.2">Joel iii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen12507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12508" type="x-p"/> 4. The equity of this victory: <hi type="italic">He shall judge among them.</hi> It is not a military execution, which is done in fury, but a judicial one. Before he condemns and slays, he will judge; he will make it appear that they have brought this ruin upon themselves, and have themselves rolled the stone which returns upon them, that he may be <hi type="italic">justified when he speaks</hi> and the <hi type="italic">heavens may declare his righteousness.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Rev.19.1-Rev.19.2">Rev. xix. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen12508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12509" type="x-p"/> 5. The effect of this victory; it shall be the complete and utter ruin of all his enemies. He shall strike them through, for he strikes home and gives an incurable wound: He shall <hi type="italic">wound the heads,</hi> which seems to refer to the first promise of the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>), that he should <hi type="italic">bruise the serpent's head.</hi> He shall <hi type="italic">wound the head of his enemies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.21">Ps. lxviii. 21</reference>. Some read it, <hi type="italic">He shall wound</hi> him that is <hi type="italic">the head over many countries,</hi> either Satan or Antichrist, whom <hi type="italic">the Lord shall consume with the breath of his mouth.</hi> He shall make such destruction of his enemies that he shall <hi type="italic">fill the places with the dead bodies.</hi> The slain of the Lord shall be many. See <reference osisRef="Isa.34.3 Ezek.39.12 Ezek.39.14 Rev.14.20 Rev.19.17-Rev.19.18">Isa. xxxiv. 3, &c.; Ezek. xxxix. 12, 14; Rev. xiv. 20; xix. 17, 18</reference>. The filling of <hi type="italic">the valleys</hi> (for so some read it) <hi type="italic">with dead bodies,</hi> perhaps denotes the <hi type="italic">filling of hell</hi> (which is sometimes compared to the valley of <hi type="italic">Hinnom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.32">Jer. vii. 32</reference>) with <hi type="italic">damned souls,</hi> for that will be the portion of those that persist in their enmity to Christ. <div eID="gen12509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12510" type="x-p"/> II. We have here the Redeemer saving his friends and comforting them (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.7">v. 7</reference>); for their benefit, 1. He shall be humbled: <hi type="italic">He shall drink of the brook in the way,</hi> that bitter cup which the Father put into his hand. He shall be so abased and impoverished, and withal so intent upon his work, that he shall drink puddle-water out of the lakes in the highway; so some. The wrath of God, running in the channel of the curse of the law, was <hi type="italic">the brook in the way,</hi> in the way of his undertaking, which must go through, or which ran in the way of our salvation and obstructed it, which lay between us and heaven. Christ drank of this brook when he was made a curse for us, and therefore, when he entered upon his suffering, he <hi type="italic">went over the brook Kidron,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.1">John xviii. 1</reference>. He drank deeply of this <hi type="italic">black brook</hi> (so Kidron signifies), this bloody brook, so drank of the <hi type="italic">brook in the way</hi> as to take it out of the way of our redemption and salvation. 2. He shall be exalted: <hi type="italic">Therefore shall he lift up the head.</hi> When he died he <hi type="italic">bowed the head</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.19.30">John xix. 30</reference>), but he soon lifted up the head by his own power in his resurrection. He lifted up the head as a conqueror, yea, more than a conqueror. This denotes not only his exaltation, but his exultation; not only his elevation, but his triumph in it. <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col. ii. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">Having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a show of them.</hi> David spoke as a type of him in this (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.6">Ps. xxvii. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Now shall my head be lifted up above my enemies.</hi> His exaltation was the reward of his humiliation; because he <hi type="italic">humbled himself, therefore God also highly exalted him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.9">Phil. ii. 9</reference>. Because he drank of the brook in the way therefore he lifted up his own head, and so lifted up the heads of all his faithful followers, who, <hi type="italic">if they suffer with him, shall also reign with him.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.110"/> <div eID="gen12510" type="x-p"/>

entries.8e1910daed64ab7298c714da39433db140c92686: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6805"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 110</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.110.1-Ps.110.7">Psa 110:1-7</reference>. The explicit application of this Psalm to our Saviour, by Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.42-Matt.22.45">Mt 22:42-45</reference>) and by the apostles (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.34">Ac 2:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.25">1Co 15:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.13">He 1:13</reference>), and their frequent reference to its language and purport (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.20-Eph.1.22">Ep 1:20-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.9-Phil.2.11">Php 2:9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.12">He 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.13">13</reference>), leave no doubt of its purely prophetic character. Not only was there nothing in the position or character, personal or official, of David or any other descendant, to justify a reference to either, but utter severance from the royal office of all priestly functions (so clearly assigned the subject of this Psalm) positively forbids such a reference. The Psalm celebrates the exaltation of Christ to the throne of an eternal and increasing kingdom, and a perpetual priesthood (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference>), involving the subjugation of His enemies and the multiplication of His subjects, and rendered infallibly certain by the word and oath of Almighty God.</title> <div sID="gen10440" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6805"/><hi type="bold">1. The Lord said--</hi>literally, "A saying of the Lord," (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.36.1">Psa 36:1</reference>), a formula, used in prophetic or other solemn or express declarations.<div eID="gen10440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10441" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my Lord--</hi>That the Jews understood this term to denote the Messiah their traditions show, and Christ's mode of arguing on such an assumption (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.44">Mt 22:44</reference>) also proves.<div eID="gen10441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10442" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sit ... at my right hand--</hi>not only a mark of honor (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.19">1Ki 2:19</reference>), but also implied participation of power (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.9">Psa 45:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.16.19">Mr 16:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.20">Ep 1:20</reference>).<div eID="gen10442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sit--</hi>as a king (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.10">Psa 29:10</reference>), though the position rather than posture is intimated (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.7.55">Ac 7:55</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.56">56</reference>).<div eID="gen10443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10444" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">until I make, &c.--</hi>The dominion of Christ over His enemies, as commissioned by God, and entrusted with all power (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.18">Mt 28:18</reference>) for their subjugation, will assuredly be established (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24-1Cor.15.28">1Co 15:24-28</reference>). This is neither His government as God, nor that which, as the incarnate Saviour, He exercises over His people, of whom He will ever be Head.<div eID="gen10444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thine enemies thy footstool--</hi>an expression taken from the custom of Eastern conquerors (compare <reference osisRef="Josh.10.24">Jos 10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.1.7">Jud 1:7</reference>) to signify a complete subjection. <div eID="gen10445" type="x-p"/>
entries.49e8dddd4bd3818b76bb0791e03da0ed0b0d10eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6806"/><div sID="gen10446" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6806"/><hi type="bold">2. the rod of thy strength--</hi>the rod of correction (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.4">Is 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.15">10:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.12">Jr 48:12</reference>), by which Thy strength will be known. This is His Word of truth (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Is 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.4">11:4</reference>), converting some and confounding others (compare <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2Th 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen10446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of Zion--</hi>or, the Church, in which God dwells by His Spirit, as once by a visible symbol in the tabernacle on Zion (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen10447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rule thou, &c.--</hi>over enemies now conquered.<div eID="gen10448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10449" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the midst--</hi>once set upon, as by ferocious beasts (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Psa 22:16</reference>), now humbly, though reluctantly, confessed as Lord (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.10">Php 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>). <div eID="gen10449" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc02f7f895c80b0aeccc58f9db2598cb99d1b2be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6807"/><div sID="gen10450" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6807"/><hi type="bold">3. Thy people ... willing--</hi>literally, "Thy people (are) free will offerings"; for such is the proper rendering of the word "willing," which is a plural noun, and not an adjective (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.25.2">Ex 25:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.54.6">Psa 54:6</reference>), also a similar form (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.2-Judg.5.9">Jud 5:2-9</reference>).<div eID="gen10450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the day of thy power--</hi>Thy people freely offer themselves (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Ro 12:1</reference>) in Thy service, enlisting under Thy banner.<div eID="gen10451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the beauties of holiness--</hi>either as in <reference osisRef="Ps.29.2">Psa 29:2</reference>, the loveliness of a spiritual worship, of which the temple service, in all its material splendors, was but a type; or more probably, the appearance of the worshippers, who, in this spiritual kingdom, are a nation of kings and priests (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1Pe 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>), attending this Priest and King, clothed in those eminent graces which the beautiful vestments of the Aaronic priests (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.4">Le 16:4</reference>) typified. The last very obscure clause--<div eID="gen10452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10453" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the womb ... youth--</hi>may, according to this view, be thus explained: The word "youth" denotes a period of life distinguished for strength and activity (compare <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ec 11:9</reference>)--the "dew" is a constant emblem of whatever is refreshing and strengthening (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.12">Pr 19:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.14.5">Ho 14:5</reference>). The Messiah, then, as leading His people, is represented as continually in the vigor of youth, refreshed and strengthened by the early dew of God's grace and Spirit. Thus the phrase corresponds as a member of a parallelism with "the day of thy power" in the first clause. "In the beauties of holiness" belongs to this latter clause, corresponding to "Thy people" in the first, and the colon after "morning" is omitted. Others prefer: Thy youth, or youthful vigor, or body, shall be constantly refreshed by successive accessions of people as dew from the early morning; and this accords with the New Testament idea that the Church is Christ's body (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>). <div eID="gen10453" type="x-p"/>
entries.adb0a375b6ac61bc2c1cda07be84adc466ef7190: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6808"/><div sID="gen10454" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6808"/>4. The perpetuity of the priesthood, here asserted on God's oath, corresponds with that of the kingly office just explained.<div eID="gen10454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after the order--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.7.15">He 7:15</reference>) after the similitude of Melchisedek, is fully expounded by Paul, to denote not only perpetuity, appointment of God, and a royal priesthood, but also the absence of priestly descent and succession, and superiority to the Aaronic order. <div eID="gen10455" type="x-p"/>
entries.43a2cab7ac0c1e976be64a50c8c8fdaad5e1a591: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6809"/><div sID="gen10456" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6809"/><hi type="bold">5. at thy right hand--</hi>as <reference osisRef="Ps.109.31">Psa 109:31</reference>, upholding and aiding, which is not inconsistent with <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Psa 110:1</reference>, where the figure denotes participation of power, for here He is presented in another aspect, as a warrior going against enemies, and sustained by God.<div eID="gen10456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strike through--</hi>smite or crush.<div eID="gen10457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kings--</hi>not common men, but their rulers, and so all under them (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Psa 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen10458" type="x-p"/>
entries.40f6f9dce2afdaca38109a8a2aca8138ea221dd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6810"/><div sID="gen10459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6810"/>6. The person is again changed. The Messiah's conquests are described, though His work and God's are the same. As after a battle, whose field is strewn with corpses, the conqueror ascends the seat of empire, so shall He "judge," or "rule," among many nations, and subdue<div eID="gen10459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the head--</hi>or (as used collectively for "many") "the heads," over many lands.<div eID="gen10460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wound--</hi>literally, "smite," or "crush" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.110.5">Psa 110:5</reference>). <div eID="gen10461" type="x-p"/>
entries.e89a0d68ddb79770ebe734809c8fc9e1f8a91d9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6811"/><div sID="gen10462" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6811"/>7. As a conqueror, "faint, yet pursuing" [Jud 8:4], He shall be refreshed by the brook in the way, and pursue to completion His divine and glorious triumphs. <chapter eID="Ps.110"/>

entries.25fc1dd7693335d27022098f8608a8e1cb9735a8: <div eID="gen22385" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22386" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22387" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22387" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22386" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22388" type="x-p"/> The Messiah sits in his kingdom at the right hand of God, his enemies being subdued under him, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.1">Psa 110:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.2">Psa 110:2</reference>. The nature and extent of his government, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.3">Psa 110:3</reference>. His everlasting priesthood, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>. His execution of justice and judgment, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.5">Psa 110:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.6">Psa 110:6</reference>. The reason on which all this is founded, his passion and exaltation, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.7">Psa 110:7</reference>. <div eID="gen22388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22389" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew, and all the Versions, except the Arabic, attribute this Psalm to David: nor can this be doubted, as it is thus attributed in the New Testament. We have in it the celebration of some great potentates accession to the crown; but the subject is so grand, the expressions so noble, and the object raised so far above what can be called human, that no history has ever mentioned a prince to whom a literal application of this Psalm can be made. To Jesus Christ alone, to his everlasting priesthood and government, as King of kings and Lord of lords, can it be applied. <div eID="gen22389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22390" type="x-p"/> The Jews, aware of the advantage which the Christian religion must derive from this Psalm, have labored hard and in vain to give it a contrary sense. Some have attributed it to Eliezer, the servant or steward of Abraham; and state that he composed it on the occasion of his master's victory over the four kings at the valley of Shaveh, Genesis 14: Others say it was done by David, in commemoration of his victory over the Philistines. Others make Solomon the author. Some refer it to Hezekiah, and others to Zerubbabel, etc.: but the bare reading of the Psalm will show the vanity of these pretensions. A King is described here who is David's Lord, and sits at the right hand of God; a conqueror, reigning at Jerusalem, King from all eternity - having an everlasting priesthood, Judge of all nations, triumphing over all potentates, indefatigable in all his operations, and successful in all his enterprises. Where has there ever appeared a prince in whom all these characters met? There never was one, nor is it possible that there ever can be one such, the Person excepted to whom the Psalm is applied by the authority of the Holy Spirit himself. That the Jews who lived in the time of our Lord believed this Psalm to have been written by David, and that it spoke of the Messiah alone, is evident from this, that when our Lord quoted it, and drew arguments from it in favor of his mission, <reference osisRef="Mat.22.42">Mat 22:42</reference>, they did not attempt to gainsay it. St. Peter, <reference osisRef="Act.2.34">Act 2:34</reference>, and St. Paul, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.25">1Cor 15:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.13">Heb 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.6">Heb 5:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.10">Heb 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.7.17">Heb 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.12">Heb 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.13">Heb 10:13</reference>, apply it to show that Jesus is the Messiah. Nor was there any attempt to contradict them; not even an intimation that they had misapplied it, or mistaken its meaning. Many of the later Jews also have granted that it applied to the Messiah, though they dispute its application to Jesus of Nazareth. All the critics and commentators whom I have consulted apply it to our Lord; nor does it appear to me to be capable of interpretation on any other ground. Before I proceed to take a general view of it, I shall set down the chief of the various readings found in the MSS. on this Psalm. <reference osisRef="Psa.110.1">Psa 110:1</reference> Said unto my Lord. Instead of לאדני ladoni, "my Lord," one MS. seems to have read ליהוה layhovah, "Jehovah said unto Jehovah, 'Sit thou on my right hand,'" etc. See De Rossi. <div eID="gen22390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22391" type="x-p"/> Thy footstool. הדם לרגליך hadom leragleycha, "the footstool to thy feet." But eight MSS. drop the prefix ל le; and read the word in the genitive case, with the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Arabic. Many also read the word in the singular number. <reference osisRef="Psa.110.3">Psa 110:3</reference> Instead of בהדרי קדש behadrey kodesh, "in the beauties of holiness," בהררי קדש beharerey kodesh, "in the mountains of holiness," is the reading of thirty our of Kennicott's MSS., and fifty-three of those of De Rossi, and also of several printed editions. <div eID="gen22391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22392" type="x-p"/> Instead of ילדתך yaldutheca, "of thy youth," ילדתיך yaladticha, "I have begotten thee," is the reading, as to the consonants, of sixty-two of Kennicott's and twenty-three of De Rossi's MSS., and of some ancient editions, with the Septuagint, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon. <reference osisRef="Psa.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference> After the order, על דברתי al dibrathi, דברתו dibratho, "His order," is the reading of twelve of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. <reference osisRef="Psa.110.5">Psa 110:5</reference> The Lord, אדני adonai: but יהוה Yehovah is the reading of a great number of the MSS. in the above collections. <reference osisRef="Psa.110.6">Psa 110:6</reference> Instead of בגוים baggoyim, "among the heathens" or nations, גוים goyim, "he shall judge the heathen," is the reading of one ancient MS. <div eID="gen22392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22393" type="x-p"/> Instead of ראש rosh, "the head," ראשי rashey, "the heads," is the reading of one MS., with the Chaldee, Septuagint, Vulgate, and Anglo-Saxon. <reference osisRef="Psa.110.7">Psa 110:7</reference> For ירים yarim, "he shall lift up," ירום yarom, "shall be lifted up," is tthe reading of six MSS. and the Syriac. <div eID="gen22393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22394" type="x-p"/> Instead of ראש rosh, "The head," ראשו rosho, "His head," is the reading of two MSS. and the Syriac. <div eID="gen22394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22395" type="x-p"/> A few add הללו יה halelu Yah, "Praise ye Jehovah;" but this was probably taken from the beginning of the following Psalm. <div eID="gen22395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22396" type="x-p"/> The learned Venema has taken great pains to expound this Psalm: he considers it a Divine oracle, partly relating to David's Lord, and partly to David himself. <div eID="gen22396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22397" type="x-p"/> 1. David's Lord is here inducted to the highest honor, regal and sacerdotal, with the promise of a most flourishing kingdom, founded in Zion, but extending every where, till every enemy should be subdued. <div eID="gen22397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22398" type="x-p"/> 2. David is here promised God's protection; that his enemies shall never prevail against him; but he must go through many sufferings in order to reach a state of glory. <div eID="gen22398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22399" type="x-p"/> 3. The time in which this oracle or prophecy was delivered was probably a little after the time when David had brought home the ark, and before he had his wars with the neighboring idolatrous nations. The kingdom was confirmed in his hand; but it was not yet extended over the neighboring nations. <div eID="gen22399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22400" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22401" type="x-p"/> The Lord said unto my Lord - Jehovah said unto my Adoni. That David's Lord is the Messiah, is confirmed by our Lord himself and by the apostles Peter and Paul, as we have already seen. <div eID="gen22401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22402" type="x-p"/> Sit thou at my right hand - This implies the possession of the utmost confidence, power, and preeminence. <div eID="gen22402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22403" type="x-p"/> Until I make thine enemies - Jesus shall reign till all his enemies are subdued under him. Jesus Christ, as God, ever dwelt in the fullness of the Godhead; but it was as God-man that, after his resurrection, he was raised to the right hand of the Majesty on high, ever to appear in the presence of God for us.
entries.8b8f02519c4f0758c66fd58242f59bb1c17e5bdd: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22404" type="x-p"/> The rod of thy strength - The Gospel - the doctrine of Christ crucified; which is the powerful scepter of the Lord that bought us, is quick and powerful, sharper than any two-edged sword; and is the power of God to salvation to all them that believe. <div eID="gen22404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22405" type="x-p"/> The kingdom of our Lord was to be founded in Zion, and thence, by gradual conquests, to be extended over the whole earth. It was in Zion the preaching of the Gospel first began; and it is by the Gospel that Christ rules, even in the midst of his enemies; for the Gospel extends a moralizing influence over multitudes who do not receive it to their salvation.
entries.56aa0142b6ee2a5ba80e86d81b7fdf51dcb04d88: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22406" type="x-p"/> Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power - This verse has been wofully perverted. It has been supposed to point out the irresistible operation of the grace of God on the souls of the elect, thereby making them willing to receive Christ as their Savior. Now, whether this doctrine be true or false it is not in this text, nor can it receive the smallest countenance from it. There has been much spoken against the doctrine of what is called free will by persons who seem not to have understood the term. Will is a free principle. Free will is as absurd as bound will, it is not will if it be not free; and if it be bound it is no will. Volition is essential to the being of the soul, and to all rational and intellectual beings. This is the most essential discrimination between matter and spirit. Matter can have no choice; Spirit has. Ratiocination is essential to intellect; and from these volition is inseparable. God uniformly treats man as a free agent; and on this principle the whole of Divine revelation is constructed, as is also the doctrine of future rewards and punishments. If man be forced to believe, he believes not at all; it is the forcing power that believes, not the machine forced. If he be forced to obey, it is the forcing power that obeys; and he, as a machine, shows only the effect of this irresistible force. If man be incapable of willing good, and nilling evil, he is incapable of being saved as a rational being; and if he acts only under an overwhelming compulsion, he is as incapable of being damned. In short, this doctrine reduces him either to a punctum stans, which by the vis inertiae is incapable of being moved but as acted upon by foreign influence; or, as an intellectual being, to nonentity. "But if the text supports the doctrine laid upon it, vain are all these reasonings." Granted. Let us examine the text. The Hebrew words are the following: עמך נדבת ביום חילך ammecha nedaboth beyom cheylecha, which literally translated are, Thy princely people, or free people, in the day of thy power; and are thus paraphrased by the Chaldee: "Thy people, O house of Israel, who willingly labor in the law, thou shalt be helped by them in the day that thou goest to battle." <div eID="gen22406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22407" type="x-p"/> The Syriac has: "This praiseworthy people in the day of thy power." <div eID="gen22407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22408" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate: "With thee is the principle or origin (principium) in the day of thy power." And this is referred, by its interpreters, to the Godhead of Christ; and they illustrate it by <reference osisRef="Joh.1.1">Joh 1:1</reference> : In principio erat Verbum, "In the beginning was the Word." <div eID="gen22408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22409" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint is the same; and they use the word as St. John has it in the Greek text: Μετα σου ἡ αρχη εν ἡμερᾳ της δυναμεως σου· "With thee is the Arche, or principle, in the day of thy power." <div eID="gen22409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22410" type="x-p"/> The Ethiopic is the same; and the Arabic nearly so, but rather more express: "The government, riasat, exists with thee in the day of thy power." <div eID="gen22410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22411" type="x-p"/> The Anglo-Saxon, "With thee the principle in day of thy greatness." <div eID="gen22411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22412" type="x-p"/> The old Psalter, With the begynnyngs in day of thi vertu. Which it thus paraphrases: "I, the fader begynnyng with the, begynnyng I and thou, an begynnyng of al thyng in day of thi vertu." <div eID="gen22412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22413" type="x-p"/> Coverdale thus: "In the day of thy power shal my people offre the free-will offeringes with a holy worship." So Tindal, Cardmarden, Beck, and the Liturgic Version. <div eID="gen22413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22414" type="x-p"/> The Bible printed by Barker, the king's printer, 4th. Lond. 1615, renders the whole verse thus: "Thy people shall come willingly at the time of assembling thine army in the holy beauty; the youth of thy womb shall be as the morning dew." <div eID="gen22414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22415" type="x-p"/> By the authors of the Universal History, vol. iii., p. 223, the whole passage is thus explained: "The Lord shall send the rod, or scepter, of thy power out of Sion," i.e., out of the tribe of Judah: compare <reference osisRef="Gen.49.20">Gen 49:20</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.78.68">Psa 78:68</reference>. "Rule thou over thy free-will people;" for none, but such are fit to be Christ's subjects: see <reference osisRef="Mat.11.29">Mat 11:29</reference>. "In the midst of thine enemies," Jews and heathens; or, in a spiritual sense, the world, the flesh, and the devil. "In the day of thy power," i.e., when all power shall be given him, both in heaven and earth; <reference osisRef="Mat.28.18">Mat 28:18</reference>. "In the beauties of holiness," which is the peculiar characteristic of Christ's reign, and of his religion. <div eID="gen22415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22416" type="x-p"/> None of the ancient Versions, nor of our modern translations, give any sense to the words that countenances the doctrine above referred to; it merely expresses the character of the people who shall constitute the kingdom of Christ. נדב nadab signifies to be free, liberal, willing, noble; and especially liberality in bringing offerings to the Lord, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.2">Exo 25:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.35.21">Exo 35:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.35.29">Exo 35:29</reference>. And נדיב nadib signifies a nobleman, a prince, <reference osisRef="Job.21.8">Job 21:8</reference>; and also liberality. נדבה nedabah signifies a free-will offering - an offering made by superabundant gratitude; one not commanded: see <reference osisRef="Exo.36.3">Exo 36:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">Lev 7:16</reference>, and elsewhere. Now the עם נדבות am nedaboth is the people of liberality - the princely, noble, and generous people; Christ's real subjects; his own children, who form his Church, and are the salt of the world; the bountiful people, who live only to get good from God that they may do good to man. Is there, has there ever been, any religion under heaven that has produced the liberality, the kindness, the charity, that characterize Christianity? Well may the followers of Christ be termed the am nedaboth - the cheerfully beneficent people. They hear his call, come freely, stay willingly, act nobly, live purely, and obey cheerfully. <div eID="gen22416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22417" type="x-p"/> The day of Christ's power is the time of the Gospel, the reign of the Holy Spirit in the souls of his people. Whenever and wherever the Gospel is preached in sincerity and purity, then and there is the day or time of Christ's power. It is the time of his exaltation. The days of his flesh were the days of his weakness; the time of his exaltation is the day of his power. <div eID="gen22417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22418" type="x-p"/> In the beauties of holiness - בהדרי קדש behadrey kodesh, "In the splendid garments of holiness." An allusion to the beautiful garments of the high priest. Whatever is intended or expressed by superb garments, they possess, in holiness of heart and life, indicative of their Divine birth, noble dispositions, courage, etc. Their garb is such as becomes the children of so great a King. Or, They shall appear on the mountains of holiness, bringing glad tidings to Zion. <div eID="gen22418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22419" type="x-p"/> From the womb of the morning - As the dew flows from the womb of the morning, so shall all the godly from thee. They are the dew of thy youth; they are the offspring of thy own nativity. As the human nature of our Lord was begotten by the creative energy of God in the womb of the Virgin; so the followers of God are born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but by the Divine Spirit. <div eID="gen22419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22420" type="x-p"/> Youth may be put here, not only for young men, but for soldiers; - so the Trojana juventus "the Trojan troops," or soldiers, in Virgil, Aen. 1: ver. 467; - and for persons, courageous, heroic, strong, active, and vigorous. Such were the apostles, and first preachers of the Gospel; and, indeed, all genuine Christians. They may be fully compared to dew, for the following reasons: - <div eID="gen22420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22421" type="x-p"/> 1. Like dew, they had their origin from heaven. <div eID="gen22421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22422" type="x-p"/> 2. Like dew, they fructified the earth. <div eID="gen22422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22423" type="x-p"/> 3. Like dew, they were innumerable. <div eID="gen22423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22424" type="x-p"/> 4. Like dew, they were diffused over the earth. <div eID="gen22424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22425" type="x-p"/> 5. Like dew, they came from the morning; the dawn, the beginning of the Gospel day of salvation. <div eID="gen22425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22426" type="x-p"/> 1. As the morning arises in the East, and the sun, which produces it, proceeds to the West; so was the coming of the Son of man, and of his disciples and apostles. <div eID="gen22426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22427" type="x-p"/> 2. They began in the East - Asia Proper and Asia Minor; and shone unto the West - Europe, America, etc. Scarcely any part of the world has been hidden from the bright and enlivening power of the Sun of Righteousness; and now this glorious sun is walking in the greatness of its strength. <div eID="gen22427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22428" type="x-p"/> Saw ye not the cloud arise, <div eID="gen22428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22429" type="x-p"/> Little as a human hand? <div eID="gen22429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22430" type="x-p"/> Now it spreads along the skies, <div eID="gen22430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22431" type="x-p"/> Hangs o'er all the thirsty land. <div eID="gen22431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22432" type="x-p"/> Lo, the promise of a shower <div eID="gen22432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22433" type="x-p"/> Drops already from above; <div eID="gen22433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22434" type="x-p"/> But the Lord will shortly pour <div eID="gen22434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22435" type="x-p"/> All the spirit of his love. <div eID="gen22435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22436" type="x-p"/> The heavenly dew is dropping every where from the womb of the morning; and all the ends of the earth are about to see the salvation of God.
entries.80118fed238627f6ab9b902bea43e86f4c1c1d33: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen22436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22437" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath sworn - Has most firmly purposed, and will most certainly perform it, feeling himself bound by his purpose, as an honest man would by his oath. <div eID="gen22437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22438" type="x-p"/> And will not repent - Will never change this purpose; it is perfectly without condition, and without contingency. Nothing is left here to the will of man or angel. Christ shall be incarnated, and the Gospel of his salvation shall be preached over the whole earth. This is an irresistible decree of that God who loves mankind. <div eID="gen22438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22439" type="x-p"/> Thou art a priest for ever - The word כהן cohen signifies, not only a priest, but also a prince; as, in the patriarchal times, most heads of families had and exercised both political and sacerdotal authority over all their descendants. Every priest had a threefold office: <div eID="gen22439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22440" type="x-p"/> 1. He was an instructor of the family or tribe over which he presided. <div eID="gen22440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22441" type="x-p"/> 2. He offered sacrifices for the sins of the people, to reconcile them to God, and give them access to his presence. <div eID="gen22441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22442" type="x-p"/> 3. He was their mediator, and interceded for them. So is Christ, the grand, the universal Instructor, by his word and Spirit; the Lamb of God, who, by his sacrificial offering of himself, takes away the sin of the world, and still continues to exhibit himself before the throne in his sacrificial character; and also the great Mediator between God and man: and in these characters he is a Priest for ever. He will instruct, apply the sacrificial offering, and intercede for man, till time shall be no more. <div eID="gen22442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22443" type="x-p"/> After the order of Melchizedek - For the elucidation of this point, the reader is requested to refer to the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.14.18">Gen 14:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.19">Gen 14:19</reference>, and to the observations at the end of that chapter, where the subject, relative to the person, name, and office of this ancient king, is fully discussed; and it will be necessary to read that note, etc., as if appended to this place. <div eID="gen22443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22444" type="x-p"/> Melchizedek was king of Salem, that is, king of Jerusalem; for Salem was its ancient name: but שלם salem signifies peace, and צדק tsedek, righteousness. Christ is styled the Prince of peace; and he is the king that rules in the empire of righteousness; and all peace and righteousness proceed from him, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.2">Heb 7:2</reference>. <div eID="gen22444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22445" type="x-p"/> He is priest after the order of Melchizedek - after his pattern; in the same kind or manner of way in which this ancient king was priest. <div eID="gen22445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22446" type="x-p"/> Calmet properly observes that there were three orders of priesthood. <div eID="gen22446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22447" type="x-p"/> 1. That of royalty. All ancient kings being, in virture of their office, priests also. This seems to have been considered as the natural right of royalty, as it obtained in almost every nation of the earth, from the beginning of the world down to the end of the Roman empire. <div eID="gen22447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22448" type="x-p"/> 2. That of the first-born. This right appertained naturally to Reuben, as the first-born in the family of Jacob. <div eID="gen22448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22449" type="x-p"/> 3. That of the Levites, instituted by God himself, and taken from Reuben, because of his transgression. The Levitical priesthood ended with the Jewish polity; and that also of the first-born, which had been absorbed in it. <div eID="gen22449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22450" type="x-p"/> This order, therefore, was not perpetual; it was intended to last only for a time. But that of royalty is perpetual, though not now in general use, because founded in what is called natural right. It is, therefore, according to this most ancient order, that Christ is a Priest for ever. The kings of England as heads of the Church appointing all bishops, continue to assume, in a certain way, this original right. <div eID="gen22450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22451" type="x-p"/> Melchizedek is said to be "without father without mother, without beginning of days, or end of life." We have no account of his parents; nothing of his birth; nothing of his death. Christ, as to his Divine nature, is without father or mother, and without beginning of days; nor can he have any end. Other priests could not continue by reason of death; but he is the Eternal, he cannot die, and therefore can have no successor: "He is a priest For Ever." Therefore, as Melchizedek was a priest and a king, and had no successor, so shall Christ be: of the increase and government of his kingdom there shall be no end. <div eID="gen22451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22452" type="x-p"/> Melchizedek was priest of the Most High God; and consequently not of one people or nation, but of the universe. Aaron was priest of one people, and for a time only; Jesus is priest of all mankind, and for ever. He tasted death for every man; he is the King eternal; he has the keys of hell and of death. As God is the King and Governor of all human beings, Christ, being the priest of the Most High God, must also be the priest for and over all whom this most high God made and governs; and therefore he is the priest, the atoning sacrifice, of the whole human race. In this the main similitude consists between the order of Melchizedek and that of Christ.
entries.cf7ef737464ecb00696df59540b3544421227732: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen22452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22453" type="x-p"/> The Lord at thy right hand - Here Venema thinks the Psalm speaks of David. As Jesus is at the right hand of God, so he will be at thy hand, giving thee all the support and comfort requisite. <div eID="gen22453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22454" type="x-p"/> Shall strike through kings - As he did in the case of Abraham, Genesis 14:1-16, (for to this there seems to be an allusion), where he smote four kings, and filled the pits with the dead bodies of their troops. That the allusion is to the above transaction seems the most probable because in the same chapter, where the defeat of the four kings is mentioned, we have the account of Melehizedek coming to meet Abraham, and receiving the tenth of the spoils.
entries.a52f46cffeb6e8fe19348844d02d342690490cf3: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen22454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22455" type="x-p"/> He shall judge among the heathen - David shall greatly extend his dominion, and rule over the Idumeans, Moabites, Philistines, etc. <div eID="gen22455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22456" type="x-p"/> He shall fill - with the dead bodies - He shall fill pits - make heaps of slain; there shall be an immense slaughter among his enemies. <div eID="gen22456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22457" type="x-p"/> He shall wound the heads - He shall so bring down the power of all the neighboring kings, as to cause them to acknowledge him as their lord, and pay him tribute.
entries.0415c38f17adf9b6cac5cefd0696c17bb6e41b43: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22458" type="x-p"/> He shall drink of the brook in the way - He shall have sore travail, and but little ease and refreshment: but he shall still go on from conquering to conquer. <div eID="gen22458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22459" type="x-p"/> Therefore shall he lift up the head - Or his head. He shall succeed in all his enterprises, and at last be peaceably settled in his ample dominions. <div eID="gen22459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22460" type="x-p"/> But these verses, as well as the former, may be applied to our Lord. The fifth verse may be an address to Jehovah: Adonai at thy right hand, O Jehovah, shall smite kings - bring down all powers hostile to his empire, in the day of his wrath - when, after having borne long, he arises and shakes terribly the rulers of the earth. <reference osisRef="Psa.110.6">Psa 110:6</reference> He shall judge, give laws, among the heathen - send his Gospel to the whole Gentile world. He shall fill the field of battle with the dead bodies of the slain, who had resisted his empire, and would not have him to reign over them. <div eID="gen22460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22461" type="x-p"/> He shall wound the heads over many countries - This must be spoken against some person possessing a very extensive sway. Perhaps Antichrist is meant; he who has so many countries under his spiritual domination. Christ shall destroy every person, and every thing, which opposes the universal spread of his own empire. He will be a King, as well as a Priest for ever. <reference osisRef="Psa.110.7">Psa 110:7</reference> He shall drink of the brook - he shall suffer sorely, and even die in the struggle: but in that death his enemies shall all perish; and he shall lift up the head - he shall rise again from the dead, possessing all power in heaven and earth, ascend to the throne of glory, and reign till time shall be no more. He must suffer and die, in order to have the triumphs already mentioned. <div eID="gen22461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22462" type="x-p"/> While all have acknowledged that this Psalm is of the utmost importance, and that it speaks of Christ's priesthood and victories, it is amazing how various the interpretations are which are given of different passages. I have endeavored to give the general sense in the preceding notes, and to explain all the particular expressions that have been thought most difficult: and by giving the various readings from the MSS., have left it to the learned reader to make farther improvements. <div eID="gen22462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22463" type="x-p"/> It has, however, long appeared to me that there is a key by which all the difficulties in the Psalm may be unlocked. As this has not been suggested by any other, as far as I know, I shall without apology lay it before the reader: - <div eID="gen22463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22464" type="x-p"/> The hundred and tenth Psalm is a War Song, and every phrase and term in it is Military. <div eID="gen22464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22465" type="x-p"/> 1. In the first place may be considered here the proclamation of the Divine purpose relative to the sacerdotal, prophetic, and regal offices of the Lord Jesus Christ: "Jehovah said unto my Lord, Sit Thou on My Right Hand." <div eID="gen22465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22466" type="x-p"/> 2. A grievous battle, and consequent victory over the enemy, foretold: I Will Make Thine Enemies the Footstool to Thy Feet, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.1">Psa 110:1</reference>. <div eID="gen22466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22467" type="x-p"/> 3. The ensign displayed: "The Lord Shall Send Forth the Rod of Thy Strength; the pole on which the banner shall be displayed, at the head of his strength - his numerous and powerful forces. <div eID="gen22467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22468" type="x-p"/> 4. The inscription, device, or motto on this ensign: "Rule Thou in the Midst of Thine Enemies," <reference osisRef="Psa.110.2">Psa 110:2</reference>. <div eID="gen22468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22469" type="x-p"/> 5. The muster of the troops. A host of bold spirited volunteers; not mercenaries, neither kidnapped nor impressed; but עם נדבות am nedaboth, a volunteer people; high-born, loyal subjects; veteran soldiers; every man bringing gifts to his General and King. <div eID="gen22469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22470" type="x-p"/> 6. The regimentals or uniform in which they shall appear: "The Beauties of Holiness; הדרי קדש hadrey kodesh, the splendid garments of holiness. The apparel showing the richness of the King, and the worth and order of the soldiers; every man being determined to do his duty, and feeling assured of conquest. The Lacedaemonian soldiers were clothed in scarlet; and never went to battle without crowns and garlands upon their heads, being always sure of victory. Potter's Ant., vol. ii., p. 55. <div eID="gen22470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22471" type="x-p"/> 7. The number of the troops: They Shall Be As the Drops of Dew at Break of Day: - innumerable; and this shall be in consequence ילדתך yalduthecha, of thy nativity-the manifestation of Jesus. Thou shalt be born unto men; They shall be born of thy Spirit, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.3">Psa 110:3</reference>. <div eID="gen22471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22472" type="x-p"/> 8. The title of the commander: "Thou Art a Priest," כהן cohen, a Priest and a Prince. So was Agamemnon in Homer, and Aeneas in Virgil. Both were princes; both were priests and both were heroes. <div eID="gen22472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22473" type="x-p"/> 9. The perpetuity of this office: "For Ever;" לעולם Ieolam, for futurity - for all time - till the earth and the heavens are no more. <div eID="gen22473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22474" type="x-p"/> 10. The resolution of setting up such a Priest and lying, and levying such an army: According to the Order of Melchizedek. The Commander, muster, and establishment of the corps shall be according to the plan of that ancient king and priest; or, translating the words literally, על דברתי מלכי צדק al dabarti malki tsedek, all shall be executed as I have spoken to my righteous king; I have sworn, and will not change my purpose. All my purposes shall be fulfilled. This speaking may refer to the purpose, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.1">Psa 110:1</reference>, confirmed by an oath, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>. <div eID="gen22474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22475" type="x-p"/> 11. Victory gained: Adonai at Thy Right Hand Hath Transfixed (מחץ machats) Kings in the Day of His Wrath, i.e., of battle and victory. Jesus, the Almighty King and Conqueror, fights and gains his battles, while sitting at the right hand of the Majesty on high, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.5">Psa 110:5</reference>. <div eID="gen22475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22476" type="x-p"/> 12. Judgment instituted and executed: "He Shall Judge Among the Heathen," בגים baggoyim, among the nations. He shall bring forth, judge, and condemn his enemies; and he shall fill pits with the bodies of executed criminals, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.6">Psa 110:6</reference>. <div eID="gen22476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22477" type="x-p"/> 13. False religion, supporting itself by the secular arm under the name of true religion, shall be destroyed. מחץ ראש על ארץ רבה machats rosh al erets rabbah; "He smites the head that is over an extensive land" or country. The priesthood that is not according to the order of Melchizedek shall be destroyed; and all government that is not according to him who is the eternal King and Priest, shall be brought down and annihilated. Who is this great Head? this usurping power? this antichristian authority? Let the Italian archbishop answer, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.6">Psa 110:6</reference>. <div eID="gen22477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22478" type="x-p"/> 14. Refreshment and rest, the fruits of the victories which have been gained: "He Shall Drink of the Brook in the Way; Therefore, Shall He Lift Up the Head." He and his victorious army, having defeated and pursued his enemies, and being spent with fatigue and thirst, are refreshed by drinking from a rivulet providentially met with in the way. But the rout being now complete and final, <div eID="gen22478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22479" type="x-p"/> 15. The emperor is proclaimed and triumphs: God lifts up the Head, - ראש rosh, the Chief, the Captain; as the word often means. Jesus, the Captain of our salvation, has a complete triumph; eternal peace and tranquillity are established. The Messiah is all in all - the last enemy, Death, is destroyed. Jesus, having overcome, has sat down with the Father upon his throne; and his soldiers, having also overcome through the blood of the Lamb, seated with him on the same throne, are for ever with the Lord. They see him as he is; and eternally contemplate and enjoy his glory: - "Far from a world of grief and sin, <div eID="gen22479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22480" type="x-p"/> With God eternally shut in." <div eID="gen22480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22481" type="x-p"/> Hallelujah! The Lord God Omnipotent reigneth! Amen, Amen.  <chapter eID="Ps.110"/> <div eID="gen22481" type="x-p"/>

entries.6d160112a161a6caeacab930b8cc259e6335eda1: <div eID="gen10060" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">To the Priest-King at the Right Hand of God</title> <div sID="gen10061" type="x-p"/> While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them: What think ye of Christ? Whose Son is He? They say unto Him: David's. He saith unto them: How then doth David in the spirit call Him Lord, saying: “The Lord hath said unto my Lord: Sit Thou on My right hand until I make Thine enemies the stool of Thy feet?” If David then calls Him Lord, how is He his Son? And no man was able to answer Him a word, neither durst any one from that day forth question Him further. <div eID="gen10061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10062" type="x-p"/> So we read in <reference osisRef="Matt.22.41-Matt.22.46">Mat 22:41-46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.12.35-Mark.12.37">Mar 12:35-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.20.41">Luk 20:41</reference>-44. The inference which it is left for the Pharisees to draw rests upon the two premises, which are granted, that <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1-Ps.110.7">Psa 110:1-7</reference> is Davidic, and that it is prophetico-Messianic, i.e., that in it the future Messiah stands objectively before the mind of David.
